title: One real, many names
hook: a Rig Veda line about one truth and many names, and what it does and doesn't say
carry: the real is one; the wise name it many ways
tomorrow: four short sentences. what do they say we are?

segments.voice: Yesterday, saguna and nirguna: god with form, and beyond stood at Maghar: Kabir left Kashi, and moksha is God's gift, not a city's. Today, the block's last day, and a line people love to quote.

A wedding toast, two families who pray differently, everyone a little nervous. Someone raises a glass: well, all religions are the same anyway. Everyone smiles. It's kind. But is it true? Someone may add an old Hindu line to back it up: the real is one; the wise speak of it in many ways. It comes from the Rig Veda. And in its own verse, it isn't talking about the world's religions at all.
screen: `ALL RELIGIONS ARE THE SAME?` → `THE REAL IS ONE.` → `NOT ABOUT RELIGIONS AT ALL.`

segments.voice: The line comes near the end of a long hymn of riddles in the Rig Veda's first book, credited to an ancient seer, Dirghatamas. It's the hymn that pictures two birds on one tree. In paraphrase: they call it Indra, Mitra, Varuna, Agni; it is the heavenly bird with lovely wings. The real is one; the wise speak of it in many ways, calling it Agni, Yama, Matarishvan. In its setting, the many names are Vedic gods. The seer is saying that behind the names his own tradition uses, there is one reality. That's a teaching Hindus still live by. It's why one home shrine can hold Ganesha, Lakshmi and Shiva, and the family can still say God is one. Many forms, many names, one real. Later readers widened the line, and some Hindus take it as a way to honor other paths too. Now notice what it does, and what it doesn't. It makes room for respect. It doesn't say all teachings are the same teaching. A Hindu who honors a Sufi saint can hold this verse and keep Hindu teaching whole, while the shrine's Muslim keepers keep theirs. So at that wedding? We name what's holy in different ways is something a Hindu can say from inside this verse. We all believe the same thing is a bigger claim, and the verse doesn't make it. That closes this part of the path: Hinduism in the world.
screen: `A HYMN OF RIDDLES.` · `INDRA, MITRA, VARUNA, AGNI.` · `MANY GODS, ONE REAL.` · then, large: `WARM, WITHOUT PRETENDING.`

segments.voice: If you have a home shrine, look at each image in turn and name it: Ganesha, Lakshmi, Krishna, whoever is there. After each name, add silently: one real. If you don't keep a shrine, picture the faces at a mixed table you'll sit at soon, and let each one be named, and each held as itself.
Never blended as doctrine. Respect for many names, without making them one creed: the way this history held its shared saints.
Something to keep: the real is one; the wise name it many ways. Room for respect, and each house still its own. That closes this part of the path.

howItsDone: Rig Veda 1.164.46 ('the real is one; the wise speak of it in many ways') is how many Hindus explain honoring many gods while holding that God is one; some also quote it as a ground for respecting other paths, though in its hymn the many names are those of Vedic gods.

fork.setup: your uncle quotes 'the real is one; the wise speak of it in many ways' to prove every religion teaches the identical thing. what does the verse itself do?
options: it gives many Vedic names for one reality; it doesn't make all creeds one.
it lists the world's religions and declares them all equal.
it warns that only one name for the real is the correct one.
fork.reveal: In its hymn, the names are Indra, Mitra, Varuna, Agni and more. Later readers widened it into respect for other paths, not one creed.
